section-1.title: 1. Computing machines
summary: Turing compares a person who computes a number with a machine.
The machine has a finite number of conditions, which he calls “m-configurations”.
It sees one square of a tape at a time.
It can write or erase a symbol there, and move one square to the left or to the right.

section-2.title: 2. Definitions
summary: Turing names the kinds of machine he will use.
A computing machine prints the figures 0 and 1, and it may print other symbols as notes.
A machine that goes on printing figures forever is “circle-free”.
A machine that prints only a finite number of figures is “circular”.

section-3.title: 3. Examples of computing machines
summary: Turing gives his first machines, each as a table of rules.
The first machine prints 0 and 1 in turn, with a blank square between them, and never stops.
It is the machine on the tape at the top of this page.
A second machine prints 0 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 1 …, with one more 1 each time.

section-4.title: 4. Abbreviated tables
summary: Many machines do the same kinds of work again and again.
Turing writes this work once, as “skeleton tables” that hold variables.
This makes the later tables much shorter.

section-5.title: 5. Enumeration of computable sequences
summary: Turing writes the table of any machine as one line of letters: its “standard description”.
He turns each letter into a digit, which gives the machine's “description number”.
So every computable sequence has at least one number.
“Enumerable” means that the sequences can be listed one after another.

section-6.title: 6. The universal computing machine
summary: This section brings in the universal machine.
Its tape starts with the standard description of another machine.
The universal machine then computes the same sequence as that machine.
Turing explains the idea here and gives the full table in section 7.

section-7.title: 7. Detailed description of the universal machine
summary: Here Turing gives the full table of the universal machine.
When it starts, its tape holds a standard description (S.D), followed by a double colon “::”.
Each instruction has five parts: the m-configuration, the symbol read, the symbol to write, the move, and the next m-configuration.

section-8.title: 8. Application of the diagonal process
summary: Turing shows that a machine cannot answer some questions about machines.
No machine can decide, for every machine, whether it is circle-free.
So no machine can decide, for every machine, whether it ever prints 0.
Neither question is the halting problem as books state it today, and lesson 4 explains the difference.

section-9.title: 9. The extent of the computable numbers
summary: Turing asks whether his machines compute every number that people would call computable.
He says that every argument for this appeals to intuition, so none is a full mathematical proof.
He gives three kinds of argument.
The first one looks at a person who computes on squared paper.

section-10.title: 10. Examples of large classes of numbers which are computable
summary: Turing defines computable functions and lists theorems about them.
He proves only some of these theorems.
From them he finds that many well-known numbers are computable, for example π and e.

section-11.title: 11. Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
summary: Turing uses section 8 to answer Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem.
For each machine, he writes a formula of logic that can be proved exactly when the machine prints 0 at some point.
So a method that decides which formulas can be proved would also decide whether a machine ever prints 0.
Section 8 showed that this is impossible.

appendix.title: Appendix: Computability and effective calculability
summary: Turing added the appendix on 28 August 1936.
It compares his computable sequences with Church's “λ-definable” sequences.
Turing gives an outline of a proof that the two ideas give the same sequences.

correction.title: The correction
summary: Turing later published a short correction to the paper, called “A Correction”.
It is in the same journal, in volume 43.
This guide had no scan of the correction to check, so it does not summarise it or quote it.
